doc.title: John Budd interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997 [transcript only]

title: Accompanying silent films from cue sheets until the talkies
summary: How cue sheets and a music library guided the playing, and his theatre jobs in Halifax ending when sound arrived.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: Was this where you sat and watched the film?
And so what were you using for music? Was it partly improvised?

The theater had a library of music, and with every film a cue sheet would come with it with the name of the film, the producer, the director and the cast and all these things, and suggested music for the introduction music. And then they have incidents that happen. Like boy and girl meet and love each other or something like that and you’d play — one of the favorites in those days was “Whispering Hope” that was the first time I ever heard the tune, that was on one of the cue sheets. And there were also mysterisos and agitatos © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -5-

and gallops and furiosos and different styles, just specific music written for that purpose. You see they say mysterious cowboy appears in window. One minute and a half. Agitato or mysterioso number three. And you’d look in the library, if they had it you’d try to play it. If they didn’t, make up something like that or something that you knew. And for news reels you’d play marches. For comedies you’d play comic songs like “Barney Google” or something like that. And then it was probably pretty desperate I think but it stayed and lasted 13 weeks.
Right. And then they learned to put the sound on the film.

Yes, the next year. In 1926. In 1927 I started again at the same place, the Orpheus Theater in Halifax, and part time, a relief pianist, when other guys would go on vacation — or would play at the Imperial Theater across the street, and also the King Edward Theater up in the north end of the town, and you’d play maybe a week with each of them until about August and then the talkies came in and that was the end of the job.
